title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol

hero.subtitle: The protocol that automatically configures every device that joins a network, assigning IP addresses, gateways, and DNS servers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DHCP provides a framework for automatic network configuration. When you connect to a WiFi network and get an IP address, that's DHCP at work. It evolved from BOOTP (RFC 951) to add dynamic address allocation and lease management.

DHCP is one of the most widely used network protocols. Nearly every smartphone, laptop, smart TV, and IoT device uses DHCP to obtain its network configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP is a framework for automatic network configuration. When a device joins a WiFi network and receives an IP address, DHCP does it. It grew out of BOOTP and added dynamic address allocation and lease management. Nearly every phone, laptop and smart device uses it.

sections.title: The DORA Process
sections.content:
DHCP uses a four-step process known as DORA:

Discover
Client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER on the local network (UDP port 67/68)
Offer
One or more servers respond with DHCPOFFER containing an available IP address
Request
Client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST to accept one offer and decline others
Acknowledge
Server confirms with DHCPACK, client configures its network interface
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP uses four steps, called DORA. The client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER on the local network. One or more servers reply with a DHCPOFFER containing an available address. The client broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST to accept one offer. The chosen server confirms with a DHCPACK, and the client configures itself.

sections.title: DHCP Options
sections.content:
DHCP delivers network configuration via options encoded as type-length-value (TLV) fields:

Option 1Subnet Mask (e.g., 255.255.255.0)
Option 3Default Gateway
Option 6DNS Servers
Option 15Domain Name
Option 51Lease Time
Option 53DHCP Message Type
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP sends configuration as options, each coded as a type, a length and a value. Examples are Option 1 (subnet mask), Option 3 (default gateway), Option 6 (DNS servers), Option 15 (domain name), Option 51 (lease time) and Option 53 (the DHCP message type).

sections.title: Lease Management
sections.content:
DHCP addresses are leased for a specific duration. Clients must renew their lease before it expires to retain their IP address.

T1 (Renewal)At 50% of lease time, client attempts unicast renewal with the original server
T2 (Rebinding)At 87.5% of lease time, client broadcasts renewal to any server
ExpirationIf no renewal succeeds, client releases the IP and starts DORA again
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP addresses are leased for a set time, and a client must renew the lease before it expires to keep its address. At 50% of the lease time (T1), the client asks the original server directly. At 87.5% (T2), it broadcasts to any server. If no renewal succeeds, it releases the address and starts again.

references.text: Droms, R., "Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol", RFC 2131, March 1997.
Croft, B. and J. Gilmore, "Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP)", RFC 951, September 1985.

subtitle: The protocol that automatically configures every device that joins a network, assigning IP addresses, gateways, and DNS servers.

tldr.problem: Configuring each host's IP address and network settings by hand does not scale, and BOOTP could not reclaim addresses.
tldr.mechanism: A client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER, servers answer with DHCPOFFER, the client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST for one offer and the server confirms with DHCPACK, granting a time-limited lease.
tldr.outcome: Hosts get an address and settings automatically, and addresses return to the pool when leases expire.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCP lets a device get its IP address and other network settings automatically from a server. The server lends an address for a limited time called a lease. The device renews the lease while it stays on the network, and gives the address back when it leaves.

today: DHCP is still how nearly every IPv4 device gets its address, from phones on WiFi to servers in data centers, and home routers run a DHCP server by default. RFC 2131 has been extended by later RFCs, and IPv6 networks use a separate protocol, DHCPv6, as well as stateless autoconfiguration.

messages.label: DHCPDISCOVER
messages.note: Broadcast, UDP to server port 67. The client has no address yet.

messages.label: DHCPOFFER
messages.note: Offers an address in yiaddr along with lease time and other options. Other servers may offer too.

messages.label: DHCPREQUEST
messages.note: Broadcast. Names the chosen server in the server identifier option, which declines the other offers.

messages.label: DHCPACK
messages.note: Confirms the lease. The client checks the address is unused, then configures its interface.

data.title: DHCP message (fixed part, before the options field)

fields.name: Hardware Type
fields.desc: Hardware address type, as in the ARP section of Assigned Numbers. 1 = 10 Mb Ethernet.

fields.name: Hardware Length
fields.desc: Hardware address length in bytes. 6 for Ethernet.

fields.name: Hops
fields.desc: Client sets to zero; a relay agent may increment it when booting via a relay.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: A random number chosen by the client, used to match replies to requests. The server copies it into its reply.

fields.name: Secs
fields.desc: Seconds elapsed since the client began address acquisition or renewal. Set by the client.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Only the top bit is defined: B, the BROADCAST flag. The other 15 bits (MBZ) must be zero.

fields.name: Client IP (ciaddr)
fields.desc: Filled in only if the client is in BOUND, RENEW or REBINDING state and can answer ARP requests.

fields.name: Your IP (yiaddr)
fields.desc: 'Your' (client) IP address. The server puts the offered or assigned address here.

fields.name: Server IP (siaddr)
fields.desc: IP address of the next server to use in the bootstrap process, returned by the server in DHCPOFFER and DHCPACK.

fields.name: Relay IP (giaddr)
fields.desc: Relay agent IP address, used when booting via a relay agent. The server echoes it back.

fields.name: Client HW Addr
fields.desc: Client hardware address (16 bytes; an Ethernet MAC uses the first 6).

fields.name: Server Host Name
fields.desc: Optional server host name, a null-terminated string (64 bytes).
fields.value: unused unless a server names itself

fields.name: Boot File Name
fields.desc: Boot file name, a null-terminated string (128 bytes). A generic name or null in DHCPDISCOVER.
fields.value: unused unless a boot file is named

data.title: Option bytes (hex) after the magic cookie
data.code:

01 04 FF FF FF 00  option 1, length 4, subnet mask 255.255.255.0
33 04 00 01 51 80  option 51, length 4, lease time 86400 s (one day)
